background.definition: Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN) occurs due to maternal alloimmunization to fetal erythrocyte antigens, which leads to the destruction of fetal erythrocytes. Complications include anemia and hydrops in the fetus, and hyperbilirubinemia in the newborn.

list.listitem: After the introduction of RhD immunoglobulin, the incidence of hemolytic disease due to RhD alloimmunization is 0.4 per 1000 births.

The prevalence of RhD-negative phenotype (a risk factor for alloimmunization) is 15% to 17% in North American and European populations, 3% to 8% in African and Indian populations, and 0.1% to 0.3% in Asian populations.
ABO incompatibility exists in 15% to 20% of pregnancies in European populations, and may be higher in African and Middle-Eastern populations.
In a study of 37,506 female blood donors, 1.1% were found to have an antibody associated with HDFN.
Prior to the advent of anti-D immunoglobulin, HDFN was a common cause of hydrops fetalis.

Maternal-fetal hemorrhage can lead to the development of maternal IgG antibodies against fetal erythrocyte antigens. Major culprit antigens are RhD, A, B, and AB, although over 50 pathologic antigens have been identified.

When these antibodies cross the placenta into fetal circulation, they can cause the destruction of fetal erythrocytes. This can result in anemia and hydrops in the fetus, and hyperbilirubinemia and kernicterus in the newborn.
Screen all pregnant women by checking blood type, RhD status, and antibody screen at the first prenatal visit.A
Administer 300 μg of RhD immunoglobulin to all unsensitized RhD-negative women at 24 to 28 weeks’ gestation, after any potentially sensitizing event, and after delivery of an RhD-positive fetus.A
Perform RhD blood typing and antibody testing for all pregnant women during their initial prenatal visit to identify women at risk for Rh alloimmunization and HDFN.
Repeat RhD antibody testing for unsensitized RhD-negative women at 24 to 28 weeks’ gestation unless the biological father is known to be RhD negative.
Screen pregnant women for other erythrocyte antibodies associated with HDFN at the initiation of prenatal care.
If the mother’s blood type is unknown or RhD negative, test cord blood for infant blood type, RhD type, and direct Coombs antibody test. B This is an option if the maternal blood type is O positive.

Administer 300 μg of RhD immunoglobulin to all unsensitized RhD-negative women after repeat antibody testing at 24 to 28 weeks’ gestation. Controlled trials in the 1960s demonstrated a reduction of maternal alloimmunization in at-risk women from 2% to 0.2% with the administration of RhD immunoglobulin at 28 weeks’ gestation in addition to the post-partum dose.

If an RhD-positive or weakly RhD-positive infant is delivered to an Rh-negative woman, administer 300 μg RhD immunoglobulin within 72 hours of delivery. The baseline rate of maternal alloimmunization to RhD 6 months after delivering an RhD-positive infant is 7% to 31%. Multiple randomized controlled trials in the 1960s demonstrated that giving RhD immunoglobulin within 72 hours of delivery reduced the rate of maternal alloimmunization to 1% to 2%. Post-delivery testing should be performed to identify maternofetal hemorrhage greater than 30 mL, which requires additional doses of RhD immunoglobulin.

Administer 300 μg of RhD immunoglobulin after any potentially sensitizing event after 12 weeks, including vaginal bleeding, abdominal trauma, spontaneous or therapeutic abortion, amniocentesis, chorionic villus sampling, and external cephalic version.

It has been recommended that prior to 12 weeks, one should administer 50 to 120 μg of RhD immunoglobulin after therapeutic abortion, ectopic pregnancy, or spontaneous abortion requiring uterine instrumentation. There is inadequate evidence to recommend administration of RhD immunoglobulin after complete spontaneous abortion.

However, a study of 644 patients who were undergoing medication or procedural abortion at less than 12 weeks found that only 3 individuals had elevated fRBC counts at baseline; 1 individual also had an elevated fRBC count post-abortion. None of the other participants had fRBC counts above the clinically significant sensitization threshold after either a medical or procedural first-trimester induced abortion. No significant differences in fRBC counts occurred between the medical and procedural abortions, nor between patients reporting or not reporting bleeding prior to presenting for abortion care. Thus, the authors conclude that Rh typing and/or immunoglobulin are not necessary followingn induced first trimester abortion.

In a phase 2 trial, IV nipocalimab, a monoclonal that blocks neonatal Fc receptors and prevents transplacental IgG transfer, was given to 13 pregnant women. The drug prevented or delayed fetal anemia and the need for intrauterine transfusions.
Suspect HDFN if there is fetal anemia and hyperbilirubinemia of the setting maternal-fetal Rh or ABO incompatibility. C
Suspect HDFN when there is a maternal history of Rh alloimmunization or other pathologic erythrocyte antibodies. C
In the presence of maternal erythrocyte antibodies, diagnose HDFN when middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity is greater than 1.5 times the median. B
In newborns with jaundice, diagnose HDFN with evidence of blood group incompatibility and a positive direct antibody test. C

Differential.Differential_Name: Chromosomal abnormalities and other genetic conditions
Differential.Differential_Features: Abnormal karyotype, other structural abnormalities seen on ultrasound
Positive maternal serology (IgM), positive PCR on amniotic fluid (if amniocentesis performed)
Fetal pleural effusion noted on ultrasound
Abnormal fetal cardiac anatomy noted on ultrasound or fetal echocardiogram
Monochorionic twins, disproportionate amniotic fluid levels, abnormal umbilical artery dopplers
SGA, abnormal umbilical cord insertion or placental anomaly noted on ultrasound

Differential.Differential_Name: Other causes of jaundice in the neonate

Differential.Differential_Features: Excessive weight lost (>10%), poor breastfeeding, decreased urine output, decreased stools
Positive urine culture, abnormal urinalysis, if severe may show signs of sepsis

Temperature instability, respiratory distress, poor feeding, decreased tone, h/o maternal chorioamnionitis, GBS-positive status, or prolonged rupture of membranes, leukocytosis or leukopenia, positive blood cultures

Low measured G6PD level, family h/o G6PD deficiency, infant of ethnicity with increased rates of G6PD deficiency (Mediterranean, Middle East, Arabian peninsula, Southeast Asia, and Africa), newborn screen positive for G6PD deficiency
Direct bilirubin greater than 20% of total bilirubin, acholic stools, may progress to hepatomegaly, ascites and failure to thrive
Many asymptomatic at birth, may develop lethargy, poor feeding, constipation and myxedema, newborn screen positive for hypothyroidism
Vomiting, hepatomegaly, poor feeding and failure to thrive, newborn screen positive for galactosemia

list.listitem: Prenatal diagnosis requires identification of maternal erythrocyte antibodies plus evidence of fetal anemia on ultrasound. The middle cerebral artery (MCA) peak systolic velocity corresponds with severity of fetal anemia. Other signs include ascites and hydrops fetalis. The diagnosis is confirmed via cordocentesis.

Neonatal diagnosis requires the presence of clinical signs of hemolysis plus laboratory evidence of immune-mediated hemolysis. A positive direct antibody test in the setting of blood group incompatibility confirms the diagnosis. A negative direct antibody test does not rule out the diagnosis and should be followed up with an indirect antibody test.
Suspect HDFN when there is a maternal history of Rh alloimmunization or other pathologic erythrocyte antibodies.
The primary presenting symptom of HDFN is jaundice secondary to hyperbilirubinemia. Infants with severe hyperbilirubinemia can also demonstrate lethargy, hypotonia, and poor suck.
Jaundice progresses cranial to caudal. Visual estimates have poor inter-observer reliability and poor correlation with serum bilirubin.
Test all women for ABO blood group, RhD type, and erythrocyte antibodies at the first prenatal visit. Repeat antibody screening at 28 weeks of gestation before administering RhD immunoglobulin.
Amniocentesis can determine fetal blood type and RhD with a reported sensitivity of 98.7% and specificity of 100%.
Detection of fetal RhD via molecular analysis of cell-free DNA in maternal plasma was reported to have sensitivity of 100% and specificity of 97% in one RCT.

Follow serial antibody titers in pregnant women at risk for HDFN. Each laboratory determines a critical titer (typically 1:8) associated with a significant risk for severe fetal anemia and hydrops. If that level is reached, refer the patient for non-invasive monitoring and high-risk consultation.
MCA peak systolic velocity, when using a cutoff of 1.5 times the median, has the best predictive value of a non-invasive test for fetal anemia.
Order blood type, RhD, and direct antibody test on cord blood to determine risk of HDFN. Monitor total serum bilirubin (TSB) in infants at risk for HDFN.
Transcutaneous bilirubin testing provides measurements within 2 to 3 mg/dL of TSB if the true value is less than 15 mg/dL; however, usage during phototherapy is contraindicated.

Direct (conjugated) bilirubin should be ordered to evaluate for cholestasis. For TSB values less than 5 mg/dL, a direct bilirubin greater than 1.0 mg/dL is abnormal. For TSB values greater than 5 mg/dL, a direct bilirubin greater than 20% of the TSB is abnormal.

G6PD deficiency can contribute to hyperbilirubinemia and may require lower treatment thresholds. Active hemolysis can artificially elevate G6PD levels. If G6PD deficiency is suspected, repeat testing at 3 months of age.
Albumin binds bilirubin in the bloodstream and unbound bilirubin is more likely to cross the blood-brain barrier. Hypoalbuminemia <3.0 mg/dL is an additional risk factor for kernicterus.
Reticulocyte counts and peripheral blood smears are typically recommended but have low yield.

End-tidal carbon monoxide concentration (ETCOc) provides a direct measurement of hemolysis; however, positive predictive value for significant hemolysis was not significantly different than direct antibody test.

A single pre-discharge serum bilirubin can predict development of clinically significant hyperbilirubinemia post-discharge. A single measurement >40% tile (outside the low-risk zone) had a negative predictive value of 100%, making it useful in identifying infants at low risk for hyperbilirubinemia as an outpatient.
Point of care testing of whole blood or serum is quick and uses less blood than standard tests, but tend to underestimate the bilirubin value by about 17 micromol/L.
An online calculator can help determine abnormal bilirubin levels based on age (see BiliTool: http://bilitool.org).

A logistic regression model with two variables (difference between starting and ending total serum bilirubin and gestational age <38 vs 38+ weeks) can accurately predict the likelihood of rebound hyperbilirubinemia.

Test all women of ABO blood group, RhD type, and erythrocyte antibodies at the time of the first prenatal visit. Repeat antibody screening at 28 weeks of gestation prior to giving RhD immunoglobulin. In women with a positive antibody screen, determine paternal antibodies to stratify fetal risk (see algorithm in ).
If antibodies reach the laboratory’s critical titer (typically 1:8), refer the patient for non-invasive monitoring and high-risk consultation.
Women with a previously affected pregnancy should have non-invasive monitoring regardless of titer.

Women with anti-Kell antibody should be monitored regardless of titer as the Kell antibody titer does not correlate well with fetal status, though a study of the Dutch population notes increased risk of HDFN with titers ≥1:4.

Check bilirubin (transcutaneous or serum) in infants who are jaundiced in the first 24 hours after birth and in an excessively jaundiced infant. Bilirubin levels should be interpreted via nomogram (http://pediatrics.aappublications.org/content/pediatrics/114/1/297/F2.large.jpg). Monitor the trend of total bilirubin measurements, which can also determine efficacy of phototherapy.
Obtain direct antibody testing, blood type, and RhD-type cord blood if not already done.
If direct antibody testing is negative but immune hemolysis is still suspected, perform indirect antibody test.

With bilirubin levels rising rapidly or unresponsive to phototherapy, order CBC and peripheral smear, direct and conjugated bilirubin. Consider reticulocyte count, G6PD level, albumin, and ETCOc, if available.
If direct bilirubin level elevated, perform urinalysis and urine culture as jaundice can be the first symptom of UTI. Initiate sepsis workup if suggested by history and physical examination.
Follow up results of newborn screen, particularly thyroid and galactosemia.
Perform intrauterine transfusion for confirmed severe fetal anemia. B
Phototherapy is recommended for hyperbilirubinemia. B
Exchange transfusion is recommended for resistant hyperbilirubinemia. B

Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) is thought to decrease erythrocyte destruction and therefore the degree of anemia by blocking macrophage Fc receptors. Preliminary studies show that IVIG delays the initiation of intrauterine transfusion and decreases the frequency of intrauterine tranfusions; further studies are needed.
The application of recombinant erythropoietin has limited clinical benefit, although studies are focused on premature infants.
Folate has been found to have a small benefit when used in conjunction with B12 and erythropoietin, although evidence is limited.
Vitamin E deficiency may play a role in anemia, although studies have had mixed results.
In hemolytic disease of the fetus, the incidence of hydrops fetalis and neonatal demise is approximately 10%. B
Neonates treated with intrauterine transfusions have higher rates of neurodevelopmental impairment. B

Neonates treated with intrauterine transfusions have altered cardiovascular development, but long-term sequelae of this is unknown. C Neurodevelopmental impairment (cerebral palsy, severe developmental delay, bilateral blindness, deafness) was increased over the baseline population in a small Dutch study. B

There are limited data that found reduced myocardial mass in childhood, smaller left ventricular volumes, increased left ventricular wall thickness, and decreased myocardial perfusion at rest. Long-term significance is unclear. C
